requirements.requirement: curl package is locked/held at its currently installed version on node1
requirements.summary: curl-7.76.1-31.el9 was identified as the installed version, the versionlock plugin was installed, and `dnf versionlock add curl` pinned exactly that version, confirmed present in versionlock list both before and after the subsequent update.

requirements.requirement: A system update leaves curl at its held version (functional proof, not just configuration)
requirements.summary: A dry run showed curl excluded from the 207-package pending set (only libcurl listed, not curl). A real `dnf update -y` was then executed to completion (224 packages including a new kernel and libcurl 7.76.1-40.el9_8.5), and curl was directly confirmed still at 7.76.1-31.el9 afterward, demonstrating the hold worked under an actual update rather than only a simulated one.

overall_summary: The executor correctly pinned curl to its installed version 7.76.1-31.el9 via dnf versionlock and directly proved the hold survives a real system update (224 packages upgraded, including kernel and libcurl, while curl itself stayed pinned). The mandatory node-restart evidence protocol was also fully and coherently demonstrated: baseline boot_id/health captured, reboot issued and acknowledged, a new boot_id observed post-reboot, and the system returned to a healthy state (running, 0 failed units) with the curl hold intact afterward. Both fixed lifecycle snapshots corroborate the boot-identity change and the absence of failed services before and after.
limitations: Minor leftover temp files (/tmp/update.log, /tmp/update.pid) were not cleaned up after the update completed, though this has no functional or security impact.

Post-restart health check first returned 'starting' and only reached 'running' after an additional 10-second sleep; this is a normal boot transition and not treated as a failure, but the window observed is narrow.

operational_hygiene.summary: All state-changing commands were purposeful: installing the versionlock plugin (prerequisite), applying the lock (core task), and running a real `dnf update -y` (necessary functional proof of the hold, not just a dry run) followed by the mandated restart protocol. The one minor issue is that /tmp/update.log and /tmp/update.pid, created to background and poll the update job, were left behind after the after-executor snapshot rather than cleaned up (cmd-85f20709627e4524, visible as residue in the after_executor temporary-files observation). This is low-risk, non-destructive residue in /tmp with no security or functional impact. No conflicting services, no failed units, no unsafe exposure, and package state is healthy post-update and post-reboot.
